To meet its statutory mandate as the ultimate governing authority for the University of Rhode Island, the Board of Trustees performs a number of critical functions, including but not limited to: (a) Appointment and evaluation of the President of the University (“President”); (b) Recommend trustees for appointment in accordance with RIGL Section 16- 32-2.2 and Section 2.2 hereof. (c) Review and approval of the Strategic Plan and the three-year funding plan for the University, which is to be developed and submitted to the Board by the President; (d) Upon receipt of the recommendations of the President and appropriate faculty bodies, approval of the awarding and revocation of degrees, including honorary degrees, diplomas, certificates, and honors to be conferred by the President; (e) Approval of recommendations made by the President regarding the awarding of tenure to qualified members of the University faculty; (f) Review of the University’s performance under the institution’s Strategic Plan developed and reported by the President and University community; (g) Stewardship of University physical, financial, and human resources consistent with the provisions of all applicable statutes and regulations and policies of the Board of Trustees; (h) Promoting and enforcing integrity and effectiveness of all aspects of the University’s budgeting and financial management, including changes in tuition and fees, submission and approval of the University’s annual budget and three-year financial projections; (i) Approve the creation or termination of new academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools and colleges based on the recommendations of the President who shall have followed the appropriate University process.

3 Article II Membership 2.1 Membership.
The membership of the Board shall consist of seventeen (17) voting members and five (5) non-voting members, including one (1) URI faculty member and one (1) URI student to be appointed by the President, and the President, the chair of the Rhode Island Board of Education and the chair of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education serving ex officio. 2.2 Appointment.
The members shall be appointed in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2, which specifies that the governor will appoint the members with the advice and consent of the senate, and with due consideration to recommendations from the President and the chair of the Board.
At least three (3) of the members appointed by the governor shall be residents of the State of Rhode Island, at least one (1) of those members shall be selected after due consideration of a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives, and at least one (1) of those members shall be selected after due consideration of a list of names of at least five (5) individuals submitted by the president of the senate. 2.3 Appointments of the President.

The President will appoint one (1) faculty member who shall serve in a non-voting capacity for a single two (2) year term and one (1) student member who shall be a full-time student in good standing at the University who shall serve in a non-voting capacity for up to two (2) one-year terms. 2.4 Initial Terms.
Six (6) of the members initially appointed pursuant to RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 shall serve terms of three (3) years; seven (7) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of two (2) years, including the member appointed from the list submitted by the speaker of the house of representatives and the member appointed from the list submitted by the president of the senate; and four (4) members initially appointed pursuant to this section shall serve terms of one (1) year. 2.5 Terms.
After the initial terms of appointment have expired, the governor shall appoint members as provided in Section 2.2 hereof for terms of three (3) years and members shall be eligible for reappointment.

4 2.6 Removal.
Public members shall be removable by the governor for cause only, and removal solely for partisan or personal reasons unrelated to capacity or fitness for the office shall be unlawful.
In making decisions to remove a member, the governor shall give due consideration to recommendations from the chair of the Board.
RIGL Section 16-32-2.2 (d) provides details about the process for removal for cause. 2.7 Vacancies.
If a vacancy occurs because of death, resignation, or removal among board members appointed by the governor, the secretary of the Board shall inform the governor of the vacancy, and the governor shall make an appointment of a member to serve the unexpired term.
If a vacancy occurs among the non-voting faculty or student Board members, the secretary of the Board shall inform the President of the vacancy so the unexpired term may be filled as provided in the bylaws.
If a vacancy occurs because a member’s term has expired, that member shall serve until a successor is appointed. 2.8 Compensation.
Board members shall receive no compensation for their service on the Board. 2.9 Conflicts of interest.

Board members are subject to the State Code of Ethics and shall sign annually a statement documenting the absence of any conflicts of interest.
Board members shall disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest that they may have relating to any matter under the jurisdiction of the Board and shall recuse themselves from discussion or action on any such matter.
No member of the Board (with the exception of the President and the non-voting faculty member and student member) shall be employed in any position under the jurisdiction of the Board, nor contract in any manner for any purpose with the Board or the University; nor shall the Board purchase, sell, or lease any land, property, or supplies from or to any firm or business association of which any member of the Board is owner, part owner, or officer or director.
No person related by consanguinity or affinity in the first degree to any member of the Board shall be employed in any capacity under the Board’s jurisdiction.
Article III Meetings 3.1 Open public meetings.
All meetings, including special meetings, shall be convened pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Chapter 42-46, the Rhode Island

5 Open Meetings Act.
Executive (closed) session may be held as provided for in RIGL Chapter 42-46 and Section 42-46-5. 3.2 Quorum.
A quorum shall consist of a majority of voting members of the Board, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings.
A majority of those present and voting shall be required for action.
For purposes of these Bylaws, the term “present” includes participation remotely in accordance with the Open Meetings Act. 3.3 Regular meetings.
Regular meetings shall be held at least four times during each calendar year at the call of the Board chair at the time and place within the State of Rhode Island specified in the notice of the meeting in accordance with RIGL Section 42-46-6.
The Board shall give supplemental written notice of any meeting within a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours, excluding weekends and State holidays in the count of hours, before the date as required by law. 3.4 Notice to members.

In addition to providing notice of meetings as required by law, written notice of regular meetings and the agenda for such meetings, or in lieu of an agenda, a written statement of the substance of the business to be transacted shall be sent by the Board secretary to each Board member at least one (1) week prior to the date of the meeting. 3.5 Special meetings.
Special meetings may be called by the Board chair with supplemental written notice of any meeting with a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours, excluding weekends and State holidays in the count of hours, compliance with RIGL Section 42-46-6.
Notice of special meetings shall specify the date the notice was posted, the date, time, and place of the meeting and the nature of the business to be discussed or acted upon, and shall also be sent via electronic communication to each Board member not less than forty-eight (48) hours prior to each meeting. 3.6 Waiver of notice.

Any member may waive notice of any regular or special meeting by instrument in writing signed by him/her prior to or after such meeting, and the presence of a member at a meeting shall in any event constitute a waiver of notice as to that member. 3.7 Agenda for regular meetings.
The agenda shall be prepared by the Board chair in consultation with the President of the University.
The agenda shall include

6 any matter that the Board has at a prior meeting voted to include in such agenda and, further, shall include a provision such that any item requested by any seven (7) members in writing delivered to the chair not less than seven (7) days prior to the date of the meeting shall be placed on the agenda of such meeting.
Any member may introduce a matter to be put on the agenda at the meeting upon the majority vote of the members present, provided such matters shall be for informational purposes only and may not be voted upon except when necessary to address an unexpected occurrence that requires immediate action to protect the public or to refer the matter to the appropriate committee or to another body or official. 3.8 Conduct of meetings.
All meetings, including special meetings, shall be convened pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Section 42-46, the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act.
The affirmative vote of the majority of the members present shall be required for the adoption of any motion or resolution.
All members, including the Board chair, shall have the right to offer motions or resolutions, discuss questions, and to vote.
The chair shall declare the outcome of all votes.

A roll call vote shall be taken upon the demand of any member present.
Any member desiring to speak shall address the chair, and after his/her right to speak has been recognized, he/she shall confine remarks to the question under debate.
Other than a member of the Board or staff members, no person shall speak at or address a meeting, except in Open Forum, unless invited to do so by the chair.
Except in unusual circumstances, no more than twenty (20) minutes will be set aside on each Board meeting agenda for persons, other than members or staff, to address the board during Open Forum; such persons must limit their remarks to three (3) minutes or less.
Board members will not respond directly to the topics being raised, but may refer the matter to the Board and the University staff for follow-up where appropriate.
Nothing contained herein shall require the Board to have an Open Forum or to have an Open Forum at any specific meeting. 3.9 Minutes.
Minutes of open meetings shall be deemed public records.

Minutes of executive (closed) sessions shall be confidential if the Board has voted to seal them pursuant to RIGL Section 42-46-7 otherwise they shall be made available at the next regularly scheduled meeting of the Board.
Final action taken in executive session shall be reported by the Board chair once the open session reconvenes; provided, however, a vote taken in an executive (closed) session need not be

7 disclosed for a period of time during which its disclosure would jeopardize any strategy, negotiation or investigation undertaken pursuant to discussions conducted under that section of the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act that sets forth the purposes for which a meeting may be closed (RIGL Section 42-46-5 (a). 3.10 Records.
The records of all business transacted at each meeting shall be kept under the direction and supervision of the Board.
Article IV Officers of the Board and Duties 4.1 Officers of the Board.
The officers of the Board shall be a chair, vice chair and secretary.
Other officers may from time to time be established with such powers as determined by the Board, and the persons named to such offices shall serve at the pleasure of the Board. 4.2 Election of Officers.
A majority of the members of the Board shall elect the chair of the Board (the “chair”) in accordance with RIGL Section 16-32-2.2(c) from among the voting members of the Board.
In addition, the members of the Board shall elect a vice chair.
The terms of office shall be three years or until a duly appointed successor is elected. 4.3 Duties of the Chair.

The chair shall preside at meetings of the Board, exercise the powers and perform the duties set forth in statute and these bylaws and such other duties as usually devolve upon the presiding officer of a deliberative body, and, unless otherwise ordered, shall appoint all committees and all special committees.
The chair shall execute, on behalf of the Board, all contracts and documents approved by the Board, unless otherwise ordered by the Board.
The chair serves as the spokesperson for the Board on matters voted on and approved by the Board. 4.4 Duties of the Vice Chair.
In the absence of the chair, the vice chair shall perform the duties of the chair, including any authorities delegated to the chair by the Board.
In the absence of both the chair and the vice chair, a chair pro tempore shall be elected from among the members of the Board. 4.5 Duties of the Secretary.
The secretary is a university staff member selected by the University President subject to Board approval.
The secretary is responsible for supporting the Board and the Board committees, including issuing required notices of Board meetings and preparing the minutes.
Working with the Board

8 chair and University President, and in consultation with other senior leaders of the University, the secretary plans and manages the meetings of the Board and its committees, and in consultation with the University General Counsel is responsible for compliance with all relevant legal requirements and sound governance practices.
The secretary serves as the key liaison between the Board and the President and the University administration.
The secretary is responsible for communication on Board-related policy and procedural matters.
In addition, the secretary shall perform other duties assigned by the Board.
Article V Committees of the Board 5.1 Expectations for Board Committees.
The Board adopts best governance practices that its duties should be grounded in the work of its standing committees.
The Board shall define the duties of each committee by approving a committee charter which declares clearly the purposes of the committee.
Further, the committee work should be accomplished in accordance with an annual work plan which is aligned with the University’s strategic vision and priorities.

Committee agendas should be developed in consultation with the committee chair and the University staff member assigned as the liaison to the committee. 5.2 Standing Committees.
The Board shall establish standing committees comprising an Executive Committee, including a compensation subcommittee; an Academic Affairs and Research Committee; a Finance and Facilities Committee; a Governance Committee; an Institutional Risk and Compliance Committee; and a Student Life and Athletics Committee.
Other standing committees may be established by the Board from time to time. 5.3 Special Committees.
The Board shall establish special committees that it considers appropriate and necessary to fulfill its responsibilities. 5.4 Appointment to Committees.
Standing committees shall be appointed by the chair.
Special committees shall be appointed by the chair from time to time.
The chair may request recommendations for committee appointments from the University President and the Governance Committee.

The chair and vice chair shall be voting members of the Executive Committee and of any other standing or special committees to which they are appointed pursuant to this Section 5.4 and shall be invited to attend, without vote, all meetings of other standing

9 committees, special committees and subcommittees.
The University President shall be an ex officio non-voting member of all standing committees, special committees and subcommittees with the exception of the Compensation Subcommittee. 5.5 Conduct of Committee Meetings.
All standing committee meetings and, except as otherwise allowed by law, special committee meetings, shall be convened and conducted pursuant to the provisions of RIGL Chapter 42-46, the Rhode Island Open Meetings Act. 5.6 Quorum and Action by Committees.
Committees shall act by majority vote of members present and voting.
A quorum shall consist of a majority of voting committee members, but less than a quorum may adjourn any meetings. 5.7 Committee Liaisons.
The President, with the concurrence of the Board, shall appoint at least one University staff member for each committee as a liaison between the Board and the University.
Article VI.
President of the University 6.1 Appointment of the President.
The President of the University shall be appointed by the Board to a fixed term of service determined by the Board.

The President may be reappointed to an additional term, or terms, following a finding by the Board of satisfactory performance in the position.
In the case of the death, termination, resignation, or disability of the President, the Provost shall serve as Interim President until another interim or permanent replacement is appointed by the Board of Trustees. 6.2 Duties of the President.
The President is the chief executive officer of the University and in addition to any powers granted to the President by law or regulation, the President shall have full power and authority to manage the institution in a manner consistent with its mission, Strategic Plan, and policies established by the Board of Trustees.
The President shall exercise this authority by carrying out responsibilities that include, but are not limited to: (a) In consultation with appropriate internal and external stakeholders, develop the Strategic Plan for the University, including appropriate performance metrics, for approval by the Board;

10 (b) Appoint the Officers of the University (see Article VII); (c ) Report regularly, and upon special request from the chair of the Board, to the Board on the general condition of the University, including progress on the strategic plan, bring attention to the Board any matter, including risks, that may affect the Board in pursuit of their obligations under Article I and the authorizing legislation; (d) In consultation with appropriate officials of the University, prepare the annual budget of the University, including recommendations of adjustments in tuition and fees and state appropriations, for consideration by the appropriate committees and the full Board; (e) Report annually to the Board on institutional progress in regard to the institution’s performance metrics related specifically to State of Rhode Island performance funding model and recommend, as appropriate, alternative performance metrics specifically relevant to this funding model; (f) In consultation with appropriate faculty bodies and academic leadership, recommend the creation or termination of academic majors and the creation, consolidation or termination of academic departments, schools, and colleges; (g) Together with the annual budget, prepare and submit a three-year funding plan for the University; and (h) Act, or through delegation to designated representatives, as the authoritative voice of the University in all matters pertaining to the mission, outreach, and philanthropic goals of the institution, including, but not limited to, interactions with key constituencies, government officials, and the media.

Article VII Officers of the University 7.1 President.
See Article VI of the Bylaws for information about the duties of the President. 7.2 Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs.
The Provost is the chief academic officer of the University and is responsible for academic programs and faculty actions.
During brief periods when the President is unavailable or incapacitated, and in the absence of specific action to the contrary by the URI

11 Board of Trustees, the Provost shall discharge presidential responsibilities as necessary. 7.3 Vice President for Administration and Finance.
The vice president is the chief financial officer of the University and is responsible for financial and business affairs and the physical and technological infrastructure. 7.4 University General Counsel.
The general counsel is the chief legal officer of the University and advises the Board and the University President about the laws, rules and regulations affecting education. 7.5 Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
The vice president is the chief research officer of the University with overall supervision for the research and economic development missions of the University.
Article VIII The Faculty The faculty of the University of Rhode Island play a central and important role in the governance of the institution in multiple ways, as specified in the University Manual and in the policies of the University, but generally through the work of the Faculty Senate.

As stated in the University Manual, “Faculty participation in the government of the University of Rhode Island is essential to its sound development and to the successful performance of its role in the life of the state.
The basic functions of the University – teaching and research – are performed by a community of scholars who must exercise sound judgment in the planning and execution of their assigned responsibilities.
The collective judgment of the scholars who comprise the faculty is a resource of great value which properly utilized will help to guarantee that University policy will be wisely established and effectively carried out. “ The collective knowledge, skills and experience of the faculty enable the University to carry out its mission, to develop and implement strategic plans, and, especially to achieve the academic goals of the Strategic Plan, which is the central document that guides the University towards achieving its overall goals.
This Article affirms the importance of shared governance and faculty responsibility and leadership for matters affecting the core academic mission of the University of Rhode Island.

12 8.1 Membership.
Criteria and procedures for membership in the General Faculty of the University of Rhode Island are established in Chapter 4 of the University Manual 8.2 Faculty Senate.
The Faculty Senate is the duly authorized deliberative body representing the General Faculty of the University of Rhode Island.
The Faculty Senate is the ultimate legislative body for matters that fall within the roles and responsibilities of the General Faculty. 8.3 Roles and Responsibilities of the Faculty.

In keeping with shared governance, the university faculty, subject to the provisions of applicable law and regulation and the policies of the Board of Trustees and with the concurrence of the President of the University, are responsible to formulate, review, or recommend policy and actions in the following areas: (a) Faculty role in shared governance; (b) Teaching, research, and faculty committee structures and purposes; (c) Academic curricula, programs, requirements, and standards; (d) Intellectual property and patents; (e) Academic integrity and scholastic standards; (f) Recommendations to the Board of Trustees on students’ completion of academic requirements for the awarding of undergraduate and graduate degrees. 8.4 Student welfare and activities.
The University Manual notes that in carrying out these responsibilities the Faculty Senate avoids interference with the authority and responsibility of administrative officers in the conduct of their duties.

The Faculty Senate also gives due consideration to the authority and actions of Presidential committees and joint committees of faculty and administrators as well as the faculties of the Colleges and the Graduate Faculty. 8.5 Academic Freedom.
As specified in Chapter 6 of the University Manual, the freedom of expression in general, and academic freedom as defined in Chapter 6, are essential to research, scholarship, creative work, and teaching at the University of Rhode Island.

13 Article IX Indemnification 9.1 Conditions.
Each person who at any time is threatened to be or is made a party to any threatened, pending, or completed action, suit, or proceeding, whether civil, criminal, administrative, or investigative (other than an action by or in the right of the Board) by reason of the fact that he/she is, or was, a member of the Board or an officer, employee, or agent of the Board, or is or has served at the request of the Board, as director, officer, employee, or agent of another enterprise of any type, shall be indemnified against expenses (including attorney’s fees), judgments, fines, and amounts paid in settlement actually and reasonably incurred by him/her in connection with any such action, suit, or proceeding, if the Board determines he/she acted in good faith and in a manner he/she reasonably believed to be in or not opposed to the best interests of the Board, and with respect to any criminal action or proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe his/her conduct was unlawful.

No indemnification shall be made in respect to any criminal action or proceeding as to which such person shall have been judged guilty, unless and only to the extent that the court in which such action or proceeding was brought shall determine upon application that, despite the adjudication of guilty, in view of all the circumstances of the case, such person is entitled to indemnification for such expenses or fines which the court shall deem proper.
Determination of any action, suit, or proceeding by judgment order, settlement, conviction, or upon a plea of nolo contendere or its equivalent, shall not, of itself, create a presumption that a person did not act in good faith in the manner which he/she reasonable believed to be in or to opposed to the best interest of the Board, and with respect to any criminal action or proceeding had reasonable cause to believe that his/her conduct was unlawful. 9.2 Notice.
This indemnification shall be conditioned on due written notice of any such claims being given to the Board which shall be entitled to be present at all hearings, proceedings, and negotiations relative to such claims. 9.3 Miscellaneous.

The provisions of this article shall in no way be exclusive of any other rights of indemnification to which such person shall be entitled, shall continue as to a person who has ceased to be a member, officer, employee, or agent of the Board, and shall inure to the benefit of the heirs, executors, and administrators of such a person.

14 Article X Miscellaneous 10.1 Seal. The seal of the University of Rhode Island shall be the seal of the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees. The seal may be used by causing it or a facsimile thereof to be impressed or affixed or reproduced or otherwise. 10.2 Fiscal Year. The University operates on a fiscal year defined as July 1 through June 30. Article XI Amendment of Bylaws 11.1 Process. These bylaws may be amended, suspended, or altered by vote of two-thirds (2/3) of the members present taken at any regular meeting or special meeting, provided that written notice of the substance of the proposed change has been emailed to the members of the Board at least one (1) week prior to such meeting. 11.2 Suspension of Rules of Order. Those parts of these bylaws that are in the nature of rules of order may be suspended by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of those present.

2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2021 / 3 OVERVIEW Preparing for URI’s Future THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institu- tion of higher education.
As a land and sea grant institution with global reach, the University of Rhode Island carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University of Rhode Island maintains unshakable commitments to aca- demic freedom and expression, shared governance, diver- sity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many commu- nities of interest.
The University of Rhode Island also devel- ops and maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with Rhode Island College, the Community College of Rhode Island, and other private higher education institutions.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administra- tive issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS New University President The selection process for the new University president was global, comprehensive, rigorous, and inclusive, involving every facet of the University community.
The board orga- nized town hall meetings with all University stakeholders and virtual open forums with presidential candidates.
It conducted a totally virtual search and selected the 12th president of the University.
The board is proud of the open and thorough process that led to the hiring of President Marc Parlange, who has already begun strengthening and expanding the Universi- ty’s research mission, including a University-wide call to develop a culture of scholarship and service, which will improve collaboration and communication across colleges, disciplines, and departments.

Even though he is in his early days as president, President Parlange is focusing on expanding URI’s strengths in oceanography, agriculture, engineering, and the arts, along with the importance of student athletes.
He is expected to deliver a new strategic plan in 2022 that will outline the University’s vision over the next several years, which will be shared with you and Rhode Island leaders.
COVID-19 Operations and Response As with other public boards, our work was conducted remotely and in accordance with executive orders during the pandemic.
At every meeting, the trustees reviewed the University’s response to the pandemic and supported its actions to ensure the health and safety of students, staff, faculty, and visitors to campus.
The board praised the entire University community for its outstanding efforts during the pandemic, resulting in 95 percent vaccination rate and a continued very low positivity rate.
Importantly, the University was able to manage its financial resources quite effectively throughout the crisis, and, unlike many other higher education institutions, URI has come through the pandemic quite well.

Ten-Y ear Strategic Plan The University will engage the entire community and key constituencies in the development of a new Universi- ty-wide, 10-year strategic plan (2022–2032) designed to create a vision for the future and what the University aspires to achieve.
A University-wide Steering Committee will oversee the process, develop key performance indica- tors (KPIs) to measure progress of the goals, and analyze trends, challenges, and opportunities impacting the higher education landscape currently and into the future.
Social Justice, Equity, and Inclusion at URI The board is keenly interested in the advancement of social justice, equity, and inclusion at URI.
In October 2020, the board heard from University leaders on one of URI’s transformational goals for the 21st century—to build a community that values and embraces equity and diversity.
At its January, June, and November board meetings, dis- cussions focused specifically on this issue and how to con- tinue to improve the environment at URI.

At its November 2021 meeting, the board reviewed the results of the “Uni- versity of Rhode Island Assessment of Climate for Learning, Living, and Working, ” URI’s first Campus Climate Survey conducted in spring 2021.
The report provides baseline data on diversity and inclusion and may be used to guide decision-making regarding policies and practices at URI to realize its commitment to an inclusive campus and to insti- tute organizational structures that respond to the needs of its dynamic campus community.
Rhode Island’s Blue Economy The Board of Trustees sees tremendous opportunity in marshalling the research and economic development engines of the University to help drive and grow the Rhode Island economy.
URI has been especially engaged in providing the scientific and technical basis for renewable energy, fisheries and aquaculture, environmental quality, marine and coastal conservation, and management efforts in conjunction with stakeholders and Rhode Island government agencies.

The University and the state of Rhode Island are investing mil- lions of dollars in improvements at the Narragansett Bay Campus, home to URI’s world-renowned Graduate School of Oceanography, to advance its efforts in ocean science.
Rhode Island Workforce Efforts The board is focused on the University’s investment in workforce development opportunities, including continu- ing education/certificate programs, professional develop- ment, the URI Online degree program, and 24/7 learning opportunities.
Polaris MEP , a business unit of the URI Research Foundation, is a manufacturing industry partner for the Governor’s Workforce Board providing competitive manufacturing business improvement programs to grow the state’s manufacturing industry.
Innovate@URI helps entrepreneurs and startups access the vast resources of the University to help grow their ideas and their business, with URI’s Business Engagement Center serving as the front door to industry since 2013.

2 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 3 OVERVIEW Building the University of the Future UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University of Rhode Island is the state’s flagship research university and the state’s leading public institution of higher education.
As a land- and sea-grant institution with global reach, the University carries out its mission for the benefit of the people of Rhode Island, the United States, and the world.
In all aspects of its work, the University maintains unshakable commitments to academic freedom and expression, shared governance, diversity and inclusion, and active outreach to its many communities of interest.
The University also maintains partnerships for mutual benefit with the state’s two other public institutions— Rhode Island College and Community College of Rhode Island—and other public, private, and nonprofit entities.

UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND BOARD OF TRUSTEES The Board of Trustees is the University’s governing body charged with oversight of critical academic and administrative issues, including appointing the University president, annually setting tuition rates, approving the budget, awarding degrees, and formally approving the awarding of tenure to faculty.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES HIGHLIGHTS Approved a new 10-year strategic plan The Board of Trustees unanimously approved the University’s 10-year strategic plan, Focus URI.
The plan outlines a strate- gic vision for the University of Rhode Island for the next decade—articulating the institution’s aspirations and the actions that will be taken to achieve them.
The agile, dynamic plan will necessarily evolve, enabling the University to respond to changes in the state and world, while maintaining a firm commitment to its land- Advanced initiatives to drive Rhode Island’s leadership in the Blue Economy Under the board’s leadership, in partnership with the Gen- eral Assembly and the governor, and with the strong sup- port of Rhode Island voters, the University passed Ques- tion 1 on the November ballot.

The initiative provides a $100 million general obligation bond to revitalize URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus by improving outdated facilities and constructing new facilities to support research and educational programs, ensuring that the state of Rhode Island remains a global leader in the Blue Economy.
The Blue Economy—which includes the defense industry, tour- ism, marine trades, fisheries, and offshore wind—is a criti- cal driver of the state’s economy, generating more than $5 billion every year.
By 2030, that total is projected to double.
A modern URI Bay Campus will help create the innovative jobs critical to Rhode Island’s future.
Welcomed key academic and administrative leaders The board welcomed the appointment of Barbara Wolfe as provost and executive vice president for academic affairs.
Wolfe was appointed by President Parlange after an exten- sive national search and will work closely with stakeholders on advancing the University and implementing the 10-year strategic plan.
Wolfe is a successful scholar, researcher, and educator, who skillfully led the College of Nursing since joining the Uni- versity in 2016.

At the college, she built research strength and raised the level of federal research and training grant funding.
She is an innovative academic administrator with a track record of success and led URI into the U.S.
News and World Report’s Top 50 rankings for master’s nursing education.
She is nationally respected in her field, holding leadership positions in several national associations. and sea-grant missions, institutional vision, and founda- tional values.
The ideas in the plan are intended to unify the community, inspire new ideas and actions, and acceler- ate URI’s exciting forward trajectory.
Development of the plan was led by a diverse steering committee comprised of faculty, staff, students, and community members, and incorporates input from hundreds of stakeholders across all URI campuses and the community.
The plan focuses on four strategic priorities with action items and corresponding key performance indicators to track and measure the plan’s progress.
The four strategic priorities are, “broaden our impact, ” “enhance student achievement, ” “foster an inclusive culture, ” and “power the university of the future. ”

4 / UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND ANNUAL REPORT 2022 / 5 Celebrated the opening of the Talent Development Achievement House In January, the University opened the Talent Development Achievement House fulfilling an institutional goal of establishing a dedicated residence facility for Talent Development Scholars.
URI’s Talent Development—or TD— program recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds, a majority of whom are scholars of color.
From its first class of 13 students in 1968 to the 1,100 current scholars and more than 4,000 alumni, TD has formed a community of accomplished individuals across the state and around the world.
Approved new degree programs to meet the needs of Rhode Island The board approved several new degree programs in 2022 that meet the demands of students and the needs of the state and citizens of Rhode Island.

The new programs include: • A Bachelor of Science in early childhood education, PK-2, administered online and developed in conjunction with the Community College of Rhode Island, that will give the incumbent workforce of early childhood educators accessible, high-quality, and meaningful pathways toward credential attainment, career advancement, and higher compensation. • A Bachelor of Arts in world language education designed to meet changes in the Rhode Island Department of Education’s credentials for world language instructors in PK-12.
The new program ensures that URI graduates are certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elemen- tary, middle, and secondary education. • A master’s degree in data science offered through URI Online. • A Bachelor of Science in nutrition within the College of Health Sciences.
Approved record financial aid support for students Recognizing the inflationary pressures faced by students and families, the board approved an increase in ins- titutional financial aid for undergraduate and graduate students to more than $140 million—a record high for the University.

The significant investment in URI students and student success ensures that the University will remain among the most affordable flagship state universities in the Northeast.
Made significant investments in the student-athlete experience The board approved strategic investments in intercolle- giate athletics to enrich the overall student-athlete experi- ence and leverage the considerable visibility athletics gen- erates to enhance the national and global reputation of the University.
In March, URI welcomed Archie Miller as men’s basketball head coach.
Miller joined the University after holding head coaching positions at Indiana University, of the Big Ten, and the University of Dayton.
At Dayton, Miller built the Flyers into a perennial Atlantic 10 Conference power, making four NCAA tournament appearances in six seasons.
The University also retained Tammi Reiss as wom- en’s basketball head coach.
Reiss has reinvigorated the women’s basketball program, leading the Rams to 20 wins in a season for the first time in 25 years and setting the program on a course for sustained success.

And, the board approved the addition of women’s lacrosse, adding important athletic opportunities for female students at the University.
Endorsed the University’s first land acknowledgment statement The University worked closely with the Narragansett Tribal Council on several initiatives, including a land acknowledgment.
The acknowledgment represents months of important conversations between the Univer - sity and members of the tribe, and it reads: The University of Rhode Island occupies the traditional stomping ground of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People.
We honor and respect the enduring and continuing relationship between the Indigenous people and this land by teaching and learning more about their history and present- day communities, and by becoming stewards of the land we, now too, inhabit.
Several additional programs are underway or in develop - ment to continue to strengthen the University’s close partnership with the Narragansett Tribe and support and celebrate the tribe’s culture and traditions.

Formed new board committees to advance research and University facilities The board approved the creation of two new special ad hoc committees: the Sponsored Research Committee and the Real Estate Committee.
These committees are designed to address specific needs of the University and accelerate progress in these priority areas.
Contributed to important legislative changes Members of the board successfully testified in favor of legislation, including a bill that provides the board the flexibility to participate remotely in open public meetings of the board.
The board extends its appreciation to the General Assembly for this key legislative decision that enables the University and board to nimbly and effectively address emerging needs and opportunities.

David J.
Martirano Term expires: Feb. 1, 2023 David J.
Martirano ’91 is the co-founder and man- aging partner of Point Judith Capital, which was officially rebranded as PJC nearly two decades later.
PJC, an early-stage venture capital fund, is investing out of its fifth fund.
Before PJC, Martirano co-founded Rex Capital Ventures, which invested interna- tionally in early-stage com- panies.

Cortney M.
Nicolato Term expired: Feb. 1, 2021 Cortney M.
Nicolato ’01 is the president and CEO of United Way of Rhode Island, a nonprofit agency with more than 80 employ- ees and an operating bud- get of $19.2 million.

United Way of Rhode Island invests in proven programs that address community issues to strengthen Rhode Island.

Vahid Ownjazayeri Term expires: Feb. 1, 2023 Vahid Ownjazayeri serves as chief growth and strat- egy officer at AECOM.

Ownjazayeri was pre- viously the executive vice president of the Shaw Group’s environmental and infrastructure division as well as president of its commercial, state, and local division.

Susan Petrovas Term expired: Feb. 1, 2021 Susan Petrovas ’92 is co-founder and past president of CDMI Magellan Rx and serves as a member of the URI College of Pharmacy Advisory Council.
Susan began her career at United HealthCare as a clinical pharmacist and served as corporate director of Pharmacy Services for Oxford Health Plans in New York City.
She co-founded the Managed Care Network before co-founding CDMI with her husband, George, in 2009.
The Rhode Island-based medical and pharmacy management company was acquired by Magellan Health in 2014.

Richard S.
Humphrey Term expires: Feb. 1, 2022 Richard S.
Humphrey has served as Little Compton town solicitor for more than 30 years.
He has been trying civil and criminal cases since 1983, focusing on serious drunk-driving cases, complex admiralty matters, construction liti- gation, municipal law, cat- astrophic injury claims, and areas involving profes- sional ethics.
Humphrey has previously served on the Judicial Tenure Com- mission and the Rhode Island Supreme Court Dis- ciplinary Board.

Humphrey is appointed from the list submitted by the Rhode Island speaker of the House of Represen- tatives.
Cornelius “Neil” Kerwin Term expires: Feb. 1, 2022 Cornelius “Neil” Kerwin, M.A. ’73, is president emer- itus and a professor in the Department of Public Administration and Policy of the School of Public Affairs of American Univer- sity.
He received degrees from American University (B.A.), the University of Rhode Island (M.A., politi- cal science), and Johns Hopkins University (Ph.D., political science).
He served as dean of American University’s School of Pub- lic Affairs from 1988–1997, provost from 1997–2005, and acting president and then president of the uni- versity from 2005–2017 when he stepped down and returned to the faculty.
A nationally recognized specialist in public policy and the regulatory process, Kerwin is actively engaged in research and periodi- cally teaches courses in administrative process, policy implementation, and American government.
He founded AU’s Center for the Study of Rulemaking and is the original author and now co-author of Rulemaking: How Govern- ment Agencies Write Law and Make Policy, now in its fifth edition.

RECOMMENDATIONS ON WINTER J-TERM SESSION The following recommendations are the combined efforts of the Academic Standards and Calendar Committee and discussions among members of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, the Office of Enrollment Services and the Office of the Provost SECTIONI Guidelines for Winter J-Term Session Courses and Scheduling A. I-Term Course Guidelines: Department Chair and Dean approve. The instructor's syllabus shall reflect the provisions of sections 8.32.10-13. The Curricular Affairs Committee and the Graduate Council shall be informed of the decision. Approved topics for open-ended courses may be offered as outlined above. department chair may be offered if posted and approved by the CAC or Graduate Council. New Courses must follow all procedures for approval of new courses and must include a syllabus that reflects the provisions in 8.32.10-13. B. I-Term Scheduling Guidelines Courses shall be scheduled for the Winter J-Term Session no later than October 15 of the preceding fall semester. Registration shall be permitted up to the first meeting of the J-Term course. After the first day, students may only drop or add the course through the petition process with the approval of the student's academic dean. Resulting tuition and fee adjustments will be subject to approved billing and adjustment scales. Faculty members shall not be required to teach during Winter J-Term Session and shall be compensated for such teaching. Compensation may take the form of overload salary or agreed-upon release time during the fall or spring semester.
